title: Knowledge Rich, Meaning Poor
author: Daniel Kliger
summary: Daniel Kliger argues that knowledge-building literacy curricula such as Core Knowledge Language Arts are a real improvement on content-agnostic skills programs but fail on meaning and organization. Recalling a history teacher who answered every fact with 'SO WHAT?', he shows that CKLA's second-grade China unit gives each of paper, rivers, Confucius and the Great Wall a single day and never explains why paper mattered or how the topics connect. Drawing on Ausubel's view that existing cognitive structure is the main factor in learning, he claims that short, disconnected units and spiral design leave children in a permanent state of low prior knowledge, so content is quickly learned and soon forgotten. He sees an 'ends-as-means' mix-up in which teaching knowledge directly replaces teaching comprehension directly. His remedy is concept development: longer units, portable big ideas, and recurring themes and questions such as what it means to be civilized, traced vertically across K-5.
points: Teaching facts without asking why they matter leaves young children with trivia rather than usable understanding.
Meaning and connections between facts are what make knowledge memorable, so short, unconnected units are forgotten.
Spiral design appeals to curriculum writers who see the whole scope and sequence, but it gives six-year-olds no reason to retain content they will not use for years.
Ausubel's idea of cognitive structure implies that clear, stable, well-organized knowledge is built by spending longer in one content area.
A stronger elementary curriculum would organize each grade around a central subject and recurring themes and questions that students revisit year after year.
quotes: A mere fact, even reported with detail, wasn’t enough. We had to explain why it mattered. What was its consequence? What did it mean?
CKLA systematically fails to build conceptual understanding. It repeatedly declines opportunities to explain why things matter, and it rarely connects facts to each other.
Meaning is not some bonus; it is part of what allows us to remember things in the first place. Connections between facts help us remember them.
When knowledge is a mile wide and an inch deep, it mostly evaporates.
We remember things in part because we predict they will be useful in the future. Spiraling curriculum systematically teaches students the opposite.
Only by spending far longer in one content area do we have a chance at building clear, stable, and organized bodies of knowledge. We might also call this construction process “concept development.
Ironically, CKLA is built on the very premise that the ends are not the means. Their idea is that comprehension is not best taught directly.

I worry that collectively we are not ambitious enough. I think we got so used to our literacy curriculum teaching kids so little about the world that we are now at risk of being satisfied they have even heard of the pyramids or the Yangtze River. Progress is good, but it isn’t evidence of quality.
